For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.

title: CyberBinGym: Can AI Agents Turn Binary Patches into Real Exploits?
summary: Security fixes usually reach users as compiled updates, but deployment delays leave unpatched systems exposed. During this window, comparing patched and unpatched binaries can reveal how to exploit a vulnerability, turning a defensive update into actionable information for attackers. Existing benchmarks do not measure this capability: they expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or evaluate binary comprehension without requiring exploitation. We introduce CyberBinGym, a benchmark containing 100 tasks derived from real vulnerabilities in 53 widely used projects, spanning six vulnerability families and three levels of analysis complexity. Agents receive stripped vulnerable and patched binaries without source code or vulnerability information, and must combine static and dynamic analysis to recover and exploit the vulnerability. Evaluation separately measures vulnerability recovery through differential crash testing and end-to-end exploitation through flag retrieval, with trajectory audits to reject reward hacking. The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%. Providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset; with standard binary hardening enabled, it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks. These results demonstrate that current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation remains unreliable. These capabilities lower the barriers to targeting unpatched software and compress defenders' effective response window, increasing the urgency of timely patch deployment.

title: AWS Serverless Infrastructure from WebAssembly Components
summary: The infrastructure definitions and the code for serverless applications are often only loosely connected. This yields a large error class: the referenced infrastructure components might not exist. It is also hard to keep the application and its permissions in sync. To address this problem we present an infrastructure from code solution where we provision cloud infrastructure from Wasm Interface Type (WIT) - the language defining the interface of WebAssembly components. We limit ourselves to the basic example of an AWS Lambda function accessing S3 buckets. We build two interpreters for the WIT language: one that derives the definition of S3 buckets as infrastructure as code and least-privilege IAM permissions, and a generic runtime that runs the component as a Lambda function and provides access to the S3 buckets as capabilities. We formulate consistency properties that ensure the existence of the S3 buckets and correct permissions of the Lambda, and provide evidence that our interpreters satisfy them. We show how selected failures for deployment of such cloud components can be prevented using our technique and how a baseline setup fails at this task. Together with the strict sandboxing of the WebAssembly runtime we achieve an instance of capability-based security for access to AWS infrastructure as a further result.

title: Mirage: Provable Defense Against LLM KV Cache Timing Side Channels with Topology-Aware Isolation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as shared multi-tenant services, relying on advanced optimizations like KV cache and prefix sharing to improve throughput and reduce latency. However, these optimizations introduce a critical vulnerability: attackers can exploit time-to-first-token (TTFT) variations between KV cache hits and misses to infer sensitive prompt tokens via prefix-matching side-channel attacks. Existing defenses indiscriminately restrict cross-tenant cache sharing, which incurs prohibitive performance overhead and negates the fundamental efficiency benefits of the KV cache.
  We propose Mirage, a topology-aware emission obfuscation framework that provably bounds timing leakage without sacrificing the performance gains of cache sharing. Instead of stalling the GPU or forcing redundant recomputations, Mirage delays token emission at the gateway so the attacker observes a natural cache miss distribution, while the GPU seamlessly continues serving other requests at full speed. Mirage uses a Privacy Odometer that persistently tracks the topological novelty of prefix fan-out expansions to distinguish aggressive probing from benign traffic. Once a prefix exceeds a safety threshold, Mirage engages a two-phase policy that uses a dynamic estimator to pad the TTFT to a calibrated cache-miss baseline. On a 500-sample public corpus across three models, Mirage suppresses the timing side-channel to near the random-guessing floor, while maintaining a significantly lower TTFT than defense baselines. We further show that Mirage withstands a strong adaptive adversary and the same principle carries over to semantic caching layers.

title: SWHForest: A Structural Curation and Search Layer for Large-Scale Code Corpora
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the MSR 2027 Data and Tool Showcase Track. Code: https://github.com/halykoss/swhforest ; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/halykoss/swhforest
summary: Pre-training code language models relies on massive code corpora usually streamed over the internet. However, researchers rarely need a multi-terabyte archive in its entirety; instead, their workflow centers on curated subsets: selecting well-documented files, filtering out repetitive boilerplate, auditing for benchmark contamination, or retrieving specific code patterns. Yet, because modern corpora are typically published as file pointers and basic attributes rather than source text, no general structural layer exists to select which files to download: curating a subset requires downloading and parsing millions of files first just to discard most of them. We present SWHForest, an open-source framework and public dataset that provides this missing structural layer for any pointer-based corpus without redistributing source code. A single pass over the archive parses each file into an AST and immediately discards the source text, keeping only its structural summary. Queried locally or exposed by archive providers as a server-side filtering API, SWHForest selects matching files first (via SQL or index intersection) and downloads only surviving candidates. Across the ten largest languages of Stack-Edu (52.1M unique files, 341M definitions), SWHForest answers curation queries in milliseconds while cutting downloads by 46-72%, reducing live structural searches from hours of per-language streaming to seconds or minutes.

title: The Devil Wears Markdown: Detecting Malicious Intent Hidden in AI Agent Skill Instructions through Hybrid Static, Dynamic, and Agentic Analysis
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC 2026), co-located with ACSAC 2026
summary:
Agentic AI ecosystems increasingly rely on reusable agent skills that combine executable code, natural-language instructions, configuration artifacts, and external tool integrations. These hybrid artifacts create software supply-chain risks because malicious intent may be distributed across instructions, code, metadata, and runtime behavior, making isolated alerts difficult to interpret.
  We evaluate three open-source scanners on a held-out test set of 140 skills comprising 80 malicious and 60 benign samples, including Cisco Skill Scanner with and without its optional LLM analyzer. The default Cisco configuration achieves a recall of 0.91 with 33 false positives among the 60 benign skills, while the LLM-enabled configuration using Qwen3:8B achieves a recall of 0.85 with 40 false positives.
  We then present a framework that combines static findings, safety-constrained sandbox evidence, and LLM-based reasoning to assess malicious intent. The framework tracks the origins of findings and relates evidence across analysis layers. In a within-system evidence-source ablation using the same reasoning backend, adding dynamic evidence to skill-content reasoning increases F1 from 0.70 to 0.85. Combining static and dynamic evidence further increases F1 to 0.89, with five false positives among 60 benign skills. Dynamic evidence provides the largest observed improvement.
  The Full Pipeline detects 68 of 80 malicious skills, achieving 0.88 accuracy, 0.93 precision, and 0.85 recall. It matches the observed recall of Cisco Skill Scanner with LLM while reducing false positives from 40 to five. This system-level comparison does not isolate model or architecture effects.

title: MicroSim: Contrastive Graph Neural Networks for Binary Code Similarity Detection
summary: We present MicroSim, a system for binary code similarity detection that represents each function as a graph built from IDA Pro Hex-Rays microcode and compares such graphs with a contrastive Siamese graph neural network (GNN). We evaluate on the TREX cross-optimization benchmark, a corpus of 849,072 function-level microcode graphs spanning optimization levels -O0 through -O3, under a strict class-disjoint split in which no function key is shared between train and test. Under this protocol, MicroSim reaches 0.9972 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and 0.9762 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), outperforming Gemini (0.9332 ROC-AUC), SAFE (0.9752), and jTrans (0.9740) retrained on the same split, as well as a structure-free Bag-of-Words (BoW) baseline (0.9484). We analyze the gap between pair classification and ranked retrieval in graph transformers, showing that Cross-domain Similarity Local Scaling (CSLS) under unified tie-resolved evaluation raises GraphGPS mean reciprocal rank (MRR) from 0.2542 to 0.2559 (R@1 = 0.1639, R@10 = 0.4561), strictly satisfying the theoretical MRR upper bound. Finally, over 5 seeds with equal compute, the pairwise cosine-embedding loss attains a slightly higher ROC-AUC (Δ = -0.0256, 95% confidence interval [-0.3282, +0.2770]), whereas the supervised-contrastive information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE) loss is significantly better on thresholded classification and ranked retrieval.

title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC 2026), co-located with ACSAC 2026
summary:
Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects.
  In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions.
  Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.

title: CRUSTPairs: A Cross-Language Dataset of Paired C and Rust Solutions
summary: C-to-Rust migration is an active agenda, but no dataset pairs the two languages at the level of whole solutions to a shared problem. We present CRUSTPairs, 1857 C/Rust implementation pairs drawn from competitive programming archives, normalised, deduplicated, and stratified into difficulty tiers by zero-shot cross-language embedding similarity, with perrecord provenance and licensing. Cross-language retrieval is hard on this data, and harder than a single baseline would suggest: TF-IDF over shared identifiers reaches MRR 0.21 and so beats a pretrained code model at 0.19, which on the hardest quarter of the data scores 1.7x chance. Finetuning reaches 0.79, and lifts that hardest quarter 10x. Renaming every user identifier settles what is being learned: the finetuned models keep 96-97% of their accuracy without them, while the pretrained model keeps 66\% - less than the lexical baseline does - and on structurally divergent pairs the finetuned models are better without identifiers than with them.

title: Validating AI-Discovered Cloud Threats on Live Infrastructure: A Multi-Model, Multi-Cloud Study
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, CSTA 2026
summary: Cloud infrastructure threat modeling lacks empirical validation of AI-discovered threats. We present a three-phase methodology of multi-agent threat discovery, automated exploit synthesis, and non-destructive live validation, and apply it to three commercial foundation models on two cloud architectures, validating each threat natively on the cloud (AWS, GCP, or Azure) it was discovered against. Of 233 AI-discovered threats, 103 were confirmed and 34 refuted (75.2\% precision, 95\% CI [67.3, 81.7]); 44 were conditional (the named mechanism refuted but an equivalent impact shown through another path) and 52 indeterminate. Multi-model discovery helped through breadth, not agreement: the three models together found 2.2$\times$ the confirmed threats of the best single model at comparable precision, while threats reported by several models were confirmed no more often than single-model ones. False positives were not architecture-specific: they asserted access or system state the deployment did not have. Threats coded in advance as observable configuration resolved cleanly more often than multi-step behavioral threats (72.5\% vs.\ 51.6\%), which were more often conditional, suggesting that models more often misidentify the exploitation mechanism than the underlying weakness. AI-assisted discovery is a practical input to security workflows when paired with empirical validation.

title: Decalage: Uncovering the Gap Between Model-Generated Reasoning and Actual Code Implementation in Small Language Models
summary: Agentic code generation often asks a model to explain its reasoning before it writes code, and a common way to make such a workflow safer is to add a security instruction to the prompt. We test what that instruction does in small language models, which are attractive because they run locally and cheaply. Four open code models of 1.5B to 3B parameters generate C++ from 166 sections of eleven public requirements documents, once with a general prompt and once with a secure prompt. The secure prompt more than doubles the share of reasoning about validation, resource handling and threats, and we find no evidence that the rise is larger for requirements with security content. The code changes only in part. Among functions with a body and reasoning, the share with a check that our lexical test recognises rises from 23% to 39%, but more than a quarter of the functions remain stubs, compile rates stay low, and half or more of the functions whose reasoning mentions a check contain no such check. Two rounds of compiler-feedback repair leave more than 80% of sections unusable, and neither cppcheck nor an exploratory ESBMC run separates the prompts on the usable code. A hand check by two annotators supports the stub measure and the direction of the reasoning result. For small models, a security instruction changes the reasoning broadly but the code only in part, so the reasoning should be checked against the code rather than trusted.

title: PQC-Corpus: A Dataset of Linked Development Histories for Post-Quantum Cryptography
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues ($κ=0.86$ and $0.93$), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.

title: Feeling Easier, Working Harder: Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Comprehension
comment: Accepted to ICSE 2027
summary: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

title: Beyond AUROC: Deployment-Aware Evaluation of Model-Internal Jailbreak Detectors
comment: Accepted to the 13th IEEE Special Session on Privacy and Security of Big Data (PSBD 2026), IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026)
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in user-facing systems, where jailbreak attacks can bypass safety controls and induce harmful and policy-violating outputs. Recent model-internal detectors use hidden representations, gradients, or internal signals to identify such prompts, but their practical security value depends critically on behavior at low false-positive operating points rather than on area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) alone.
  We study two data dependencies that shape this behavior: calibration data, which determine the detection threshold, and reference data, which can influence detector scores. Across four model-internal detectors, four LLMs, and twelve jailbreak families, thresholds calibrated on curated benign prompts frequently fail to preserve their false-positive rate (FPR) budgets on real-user traffic. Recalibration improves false-positive control but reveals substantial family-level coverage gaps, including cases with high AUROC but low true-positive rate (TPR). Causal reference-set interventions show that changing reference composition can substantially alter family-level detection and that improving coverage of one attack family can reduce coverage of others.
  These findings show that calibration and reference data are part of a detector's security behavior. We therefore recommend evaluating model-internal jailbreak defenses using realized FPR on deployment-like traffic and per-family TPR at explicit low-FPR operating points, with AUROC used as a complementary ranking metric rather than the primary security measure.

title: SWE-Time: Benchmarking Temporal Repository Understanding
summary: Repository-level code-understanding benchmarks have progressively expanded the spatial scope of reasoning, from local code to entire repositories, while largely treating each repository as a static snapshot. However, how models reason about repository evolution over time remains largely unexplored. We introduce SWE-Time, a benchmark for temporal repository understanding that makes repository evolution itself the reasoning target. SWE-Time evaluates two complementary temporal directions: retrospective understanding of repository evolution through historical regression analysis and prospective understanding of intended changes from pre-change repository states. To enable realistic yet reliable evaluation in these settings, we introduce the RealWorld-to-Verifiable Construction Framework, which transforms real-world developer queries and historical evidence into verifiable evaluation tasks. We evaluate 15 coding agents on 1,661 cases from 65 GitHub repositories. Within Claude Code, Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest SWE-Time Avg. of 61.9, leaving substantial headroom. Controlled analyses highlight the importance of historical code evidence and developer intent, while consistent reasoning across repository states remains challenging. These results highlight repository evolution as a distinct and challenging dimension of code understanding.

title: Tracing MCP Security Vulnerabilities: Constructing and Analyzing an MCP Security Vulnerability Dataset
comment: 9 pages. Published at Data4SoftSec / IEEE SPW 2026. Post-publication dataset link: https://huggingface.co/datasets/XuViewer/mcp-vulnerability-dataset (maintained dataset extending beyond the original 24-record snapshot)
summary: As a core protocol for integrating large language models (LLMs) with external data sources and tools, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has quickly become a key interface in emerging AI agent systems. As the MCP ecosystem expands, reported vulnerabilities have also increased, creating a growing software-security attack surface. However, MCP vulnerability information remains scattered, noisy, and difficult to study systematically. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a curated MCP vulnerability dataset from CVE disclosures. Starting from 119 MCP-related records retrieved through February 2026, we filter unrelated cases out and obtain a validated snapshot of 24 MCP vulnerabilities. Our filtering methodology explicitly addresses acronym ambiguity and achieves 96.7% inter-rater agreement on a sampled exclusion audit while retaining all known high-severity MCP cases identified in public advisories. Using this initial dataset snapshot, we find that 87.5% of validated vulnerabilities are Critical or High severity, and that injection and path traversal vulnerabilities account for 66.7% of cases. We further identify recurring issues involving insufficient input validation, inadequate access control, and protocol-level security gaps. Through six representative case studies, we illustrate common exploitation patterns and map them to practical defenses. We release the dataset, reproducibility tooling, and a sustainable maintenance workflow as a foundation for future MCP security measurement, benchmarking, and defense research.

title: LiveWorkspace: Externalizing Visual Understanding as Persistent Shared State for Screenshot-to-Code Agents
comment: 17 pages, including references and appendices
summary: Screenshot-to-Code requires coding agents to sustain visual understanding across code generation, execution, and revision. We introduce LiveWorkspace, a visual coding harness that externalizes this understanding as Shared Visual State (Shared VS), an implementation-independent representation of visual hierarchy, node attributes, and layout relations. LiveWorkspace constructs and retains \textit{Target} from screenshots and recovers \textit{Current} from browser execution in the same schema. Structured Diff and implementation bindings guide code modifications; user edits update \textit{Target} and reuse the alignment loop. Using GPT-5.2 for both methods, LiveWorkspace improves end-to-end Avg by 1.8 points on Design2Code and 2.0 on ScreenBench over a control with matched model-call counts and stagewise budget limits. Further experiments demonstrate reuse of constructed Shared VS across coders and improvements in iterative repair. LiveWorkspace also achieves 93.0\% edit success across 100 controlled editing cases. These findings support treating visual understanding as a persistent shared working state throughout code generation, execution, and modification.

title: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
summary: Although hidden-state probes efficiently monitor model operation, it remains unclear whether probes trained on benign tool use remain useful for detecting incorrect actions under adversarial conditions. In this research, we assess this problem from the perspective of operational tool-action correct- ness. we use four AgentDojo suites, four conditions, and three models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and GLM- 4.6V-Flash (9B). We perform a five-fold, task-grouped out-of-fold (OOF) evaluation for each model. We train step-specific logistic- regression probes only on benign and non-defended trajectories and evaluate them on held-out trajectories for benign, prompt- injection, system-override, and tool-poisoning conditions. We compare our hidden-state probe to mean tool-call-token entropy, negative mean tool-call-token log-probability, and self-consistency uncertainty. The paired tests highlight six significant differences after Holm correction. All of the tests involve Qwen2.5-14B- Instruct under the system-override condition, with all three scalar uncertainty metrics obtaining higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP) than the hidden-state probe. These results suggest that benign-trained hidden-state probes should not be assumed to reliably detect operational tool-action errors under adversarial conditions.

title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code, data and trained adapters: https://github.com/JetXu-LLM/kestrel-capture-context
summary: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.

title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 10 pages plus references and appendices
summary: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring; on a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split it reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Since it monitors trajectory, not surface content, its detection is channel-invariant: the strongest auditor flags image-delivered attacks about as reliably as their text equivalents (recall gap $\leq$2 points per model). Across GPT, Gemini, and Claude auditors, calibration keeps false positives low while recall tracks model capability, strongest for Claude.

title: ForgeSystem: An Architecture for Demand-Specific Artefact Production with AI Agents
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: General-purpose software serves many different demands, but this flexibility costs performance and efficiency on any specific demand. Software tailored to a specific demand avoids these losses, yet developing it requires substantial time and effort from human experts. AI agents offer an alternative: they can design, implement and test artefacts tailored to individual demands. We call this production paradigm Forge. Forging for a demand is economically justified when the cumulative benefit of specialisation exceeds the total cost of construction, verification and maintenance. To make Forge a repeatable production process, we propose ForgeSystem, which consists of a control layer, a forge loop and a recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. The control layer selects which artefact serves each demand and decides which demands to forge, when to forge them and from which starting point; the forge loop iterates between production and verification until a candidate artefact passes verification; and the RSI loop draws on accumulated production records to supply starting points, refine the harness and train models. We implement ForgeSystem for training frameworks, decoding megakernels and individual computational kernels. Forged training engines reach 1.047-1.332x the model-FLOPs utilisation of their reference frameworks, forged megakernels achieve a geometric-mean decoding speedup of 1.21x over SGLang across thirteen configurations, and forged kernels match or exceed expert libraries in eighteen of twenty-two configurations, while satisfying task-specific quality requirements. Controlled comparisons show that explicit quality requirements steer agents towards optimisations that preserve training quality. We also discuss a gradual transition to Forge through service routing, and how demand-specific production may shift value accumulation and trust towards production systems.

title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
summary: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation remains open.

title: From Formal Methods to Fuzzing and Back
summary: For the first twelve years of my career in computer science I mainly worked on formal methods. I had been drawn to the field as an undergraduate by its promise of a way to build software with strong, mathematically based correctness guarantees. But after many years of struggling to make formal methods scale, I was seduced by randomised testing---also known as fuzzing. Fuzzing is much less principled than formal methods, but it just works: it can be readily applied to very large systems, and it is extremely effective at finding real bugs that developers care about and fix. In this personal account I trace my path from formal methods to fuzzing, by way of the GPUVerify project on verifying GPU kernels and the GraphicsFuzz project on randomised testing of GPU compilers. I argue that the oracle problem provides an intellectual link between fuzzing and formal methods, describe my continuing, targeted uses of formal methods in the domain of GPU programming language design, and discuss work at the boundary between formal methods and fuzzing. Finally, I reflect on whether generative AI might be the missing ingredient that allows formal methods to scale, and set out my plans for large-scale formal methods via the Keystone project, through which my collaborators and I aim to find out how much of that promise can be realised in practice.

title: SkillCODER: Towards Auditing and Attribution of Copyright Infringement in LLM Agent Skills
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at ACM CCS 2026. Code: https://github.com/EonHao/SkillCODER
summary: Agent skills package reusable workflows and task-specific procedures into deployable natural-language artifacts for LLM agents. Their scale and readability make them valuable but vulnerable to unauthorized redistribution and repackaging. Existing prompt copyright auditing methods struggle with long skills and introduce token-level perturbations that compromise readability. We propose SkillCODER for copyright auditing and buyer attribution in a black-box, content-only setting. During embedding, SkillCODER parses a skill into a section-aware intermediate representation, SkillIR, to identify structural anchors. It distributes conditional instructions across these anchors to form an Artifact-Gated Capsule, designed to activate under verification queries and remain dormant otherwise. Controlled-Vocabulary Error-Correcting Codes encode buyer-specific fingerprints through controlled lexical choices within the capsule. During verification, the defender issues paired positive and negative probes, extracts capsule evidence, and recovers ownership and buyer identity through error-correcting decoding. Across three domains, six models, and three agent frameworks, SkillCODER achieves 99.2% owner verification and 99.3% buyer Top-1 attribution accuracy while preserving task fidelity, substantially outperforming prompt-level baselines. Embedded signals remain robust under paraphrase, compression, clause deletion, and reorganization. Under five adaptive attacks, including a method-aware LLM sanitizer and multi-buyer collusion, ownership evidence remains reliably detectable while buyer attribution degrades gracefully.

title: Exploring public-private data sharing practices through the lens of Open Data Ecosystems: A multiple case study on municipal and regional freight logistics
comment: Pre-print of paper currently in submission
summary:
Background: Freight transport is expected to increase, contributing to air pollution. There is, therefore, a critical need for increased efficiency that can reduce emissions. Data sharing is one approach, where actors within Open Data Ecosystems (ODE) collaborate and share data among stakeholders to plan and operate more efficient and sustainable freight transport.
  Aim: In this study, we explore how public-private data sharing practices in municipal and regional last-mile freight logistics in Sweden may improve efficiency.
  Method: Following a prolonged participation process, we conducted a multiple-case study involving three different cases, built upon initial meetings, semi-structured interviews, supported by a thematic analysis, and validated through a follow-up workshop.
  Results: The findings show that data sharing in public-private freight logistics (ODE-PPF) is shaped by interrelated socio-technical aspects, including platform design, roles of actors, handling of sensitive data, data quality, and procurement processes. We synthesize our findings in an actor model and a conceptual model, highlighting how these aspects contribute to the functioning of ODE-PPF, and derive seven proposition sketches as a foundation for future research.
  Conclusion: Data sharing is a central mechanism enabling integration and value creation in last-mile logistics. It depends on the interaction between technical and organizational aspects. Public actors can undertake a key role as a neutral keystone actor by orchestrating the ecosystem and facilitating data sharing through governance practices such as procurement.

title: Agentic Attribution of Cloud Resource Ownership
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables
summary: Security tools raise findings across cloud environments, and AI agents now investigate and prioritize them. A finding is still resolved by people: it has to reach the people responsible for fixing it and accountable for the resource it concerns. Ownership is the organizational context that decides who that is. Where recorded, it is declared by hand in configuration management databases or owner tags and goes stale unless kept current; accounts are shared, and automation creates much of the infrastructure. The knowledge sits in work records, code history, audit logs and identity directories, encoded in each organization's own conventions. Recovering it poses four challenges: the signal is scattered across sources, none of them authoritative; the conventions that carry it differ between organizations; reaching an owner takes multi-hop links; and those related to a resource differ in the strength of their relation. We define ownership as a set of entities, people or teams, each related to the resource by one of five patterns ordered by strength. We present a reference architecture for agentic ownership attribution that derives ownership from these records instead of declaring it: it profiles an organization offline into tested signal procedures and an ownership playbook, then attributes each resource with a coordinator agent and parallel investigators, with confidence computed by rules. On 100 resources of 50 Amazon Web Services (AWS) resource types in one organization, we pool the architecture's candidates with those of an unprimed general-purpose agent and verify every evidence piece against the records. The architecture reaches 92.1% weighted recall and 86.6% weighted precision, against 54.8% and 77.4%, at 0.55 times the agent's cost per unit of coverage. The difference lies in people who build and change resources without an explicit owner, found through work records and code history.

title: Surrendering and Reclaiming Judgment: How Software Engineering Students Experience AI Reliance
comment: Submitted to TOSEM
summary: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. Existing work on how students and novices work with AI has mostly focused on small programming exercises or on students' perceptions of AI, so little is known about how students experience AI as they learn software architecture in larger team projects. We report on an exploratory case study of 43 senior software engineering students who used AI throughout a semester-long, team-based software architecture project. We combined surveys with focus groups and analyzed the focus group transcripts and the open survey responses through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. We constructed two themes. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

title: Attacking Slide Puzzle CAPTCHAs Based on Time and Space Generative Adversarial Networks
summary: CAPTCHAs can protect websites from malicious attacks. As a typical representative of behavior CAPTCHAs, slide puzzle CAPTCHAs have become increasingly popular in recent years due to their user-friendliness and high security. Previous attack methods on slide puzzle CAPTCHA mainly face challenges in the following four aspects. (1) The defense mechanisms of previous slide puzzle CAPTCHAs were relatively simple. The current slide puzzle CAPTCHAs have added complex interferences, detected slide trajectory features in the two-dimensional space, and added other defense mechanisms. (2) The previous notch detection methods were difficult to accurately locate the notch positions. (3) Previous attack trajectories were limited to the horizontal dimension, making them impossible to pass the existing detection. (4) The previous attack trajectories were generated by fitting functions, which were relatively simple and could not well simulate the slide characteristics of human users. In response to the above challenges, firstly, we systematically analyze the defense strategies of six most popular slide puzzle CAPTCHAs: Capy, Dingxiang, Geetest, Kyger, Shumei and Tencent. Secondly, for each type of CAPTCHA, we construct a notch detection dataset and a slide trajectory dataset separately. Thirdly, we use advanced YOLOv11 to detect the notch positions and train generative adversarial networks (GAN) to generate attack trajectories. As far as we know, we are the first to generate attack trajectories by directly learning human slide trajectory characteristic. According to the experimental results, this method cracked six most popular slide puzzle CAPTCHAs with success rates of over 90\%, and the attack time is only about 5 seconds, indicating that the security of existing slide puzzle CAPTCHAs is facing challenge. At the same time, we propose various methods to enhance the security of slide puzzle CAPTCHAs.

title: WasmLens: Automatic Glass-Box Instrumentation for Composed WebAssembly Applications
comment: Accepted article in WebAssembly, Cloud and Edge: Shaping the Future of Computing (WACE '26)
summary: The WebAssembly Component Model enables language-independent composition of independently developed components, but complicates observability. Existing tracing support flattens execution hierarchy by attributing every span created inside a composition to a single host-level parent context, so execution across component boundaries cannot be reconstructed. The problem is amplified because components are typically deployed as black boxes whose internals cannot be modified or inspected by the system integrator. To address these limitations, we propose a revised wasi:otel/tracing design in which the runtime maintains a per-component span stack, restoring parent-child relationships across component boundaries without changing component interfaces or source code. This change has since been adopted upstream. Building on this design, we present WasmLens, an automatic instrumentation tool that derives instrumentation points from a composition graph and injects tracing middleware into already composed binaries, yielding end-to-end traces for black-box compositions with no developer configuration. This automatic instrumentation raises mean request latency from $238$ $μ$s to $454$ $μ$s across six component boundaries. Raising the expected number of boundary crossings from 6 to 11 further increases latency to $514$ $μ$s, an incremental cost of $12$ $μ$s per crossing, of which $10.4$ $μ$s is attributable to instrumentation. These results show that instrumentation overhead is additive in composition depth rather than proportional to baseline execution time.

title: Self-Healing by design: Immune-system inspired autonomous cyber resilience
comment: The content of this paper was presented at MAST Australia 2024, 19-21 November in Adelaide. The presentation was accepted after review of the abstract that is published on https://mastconfex.com/australia2024/
summary: Digital innovations have strongly improved ship capabilities, including command, control & communication, navigation and combat management. In the wake of digitisation and geopolitical stress, resilience against cyber-attacks has become a key challenge. Autonomous Cyber Resilience (ACR) methods, inspired by features of the human immune system, provide a promising perspective. Proofs of concept of autonomous self-healing and self-protecting software have been realised in cloud environments using containerisation, monitoring and deployment technology. However, developing a suitable "cyber immune system" for more complex digital systems is still an intricate challenge. In this paper, we share insights on how ACR methods can be combined with resilience mechanisms present in critical naval and aeronautical manoeuvring systems. Using TNO's "OpPic" application, we show how TNO's Self-Healing for Cyber Security software can provide autonomous mission- and threat-adaptive resilience. On this basis, six guidelines for the design of autonomous cyber resilient systems are derived. The ultimate goal is to enable operators to oversee and control their system's "cyber immune response", to be able to continuously adapt to evolving threats and mission priorities.

title: Will AI mess my RTL? A snapshot-based approach to verifying AI-written RTL
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure
summary: With the growing interest in using AI (Artificial Intelligence) for RTL (Register-Transfer Level) hardware development, robust and comprehensive verification has become more important than ever. As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly assist in creating and modifying RTL designs, ensuring that these changes preserve existing functionality is paramount for building trust in AI-driven workflows. We present SVApshot, a fully automated framework that leverages LLMs to generate and systematically attempt to correct SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) for RTL modules, completely removing the human from the generation loop. SVApshot introduces a novel snapshot methodology that captures the current functionality of a design as a comprehensive set of formal assertions, creating a regression suite for validating future changes--whether made by humans or AI. The framework features automated duplicate detection, assertion set expansion, and iterative repair of failing assertions using LLM-guided debugging with formal verification feedback. Our experimental evaluation across diverse RTL modules demonstrates high coverage for complex modules, with successful detection of both manually-injected and AI-introduced bugs. Additionally, this framework opens the door for automatic generation of formal testbenches to benchmark LLMs for hardware design, moving beyond binary pass/fail metrics towards nuanced assertion-based scoring.

title: RoCoMark: Robust Code Watermarking Against LLM-Based Functionality-Preserving Rewriting Attacks
comment: 17 pages
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) present significant challenges to source tracing of generated code, as LLM rewriting can substantially alter the syntactic and structural characteristics of watermarked code. However, existing watermarking methods often suffer severe performance degradation under LLM-based functionality-preserving rewriting attacks. We attribute this vulnerability not merely to the intensity of rewriting, but to a fundamental distribution mismatch between the perturbations encountered during watermark training and the global, non-deterministic rewriting behaviors induced by LLMs. In order to deal with this challenge, we propose RoCoMark, a Robust Code waterMarking framework that explicitly learns and adapts to LLM rewriting behaviors. RoCoMark is a multi-round minimax game between the watermark embedder and LLM rewriter. In each round, the embedder first learns threat profiling from LLM-rewritten code by optimizing the watermark encoder through contrastive learning and knowledge distillation while mitigating catastrophic representation drift. Then the embedder improves strategies by optimizing the watermark encoder and extractor simultaneously. Finally, an adaptive attack-evolution mechanism based on Reflexion and short- and long-term memory pools is applied, enabling continuous interaction between the watermark embedder and evolving rewriting strategies. This iterative attacker-defender process progressively improves the robustness of the watermark against diverse and previously unseen LLM rewriting behaviors. Extensive experiments on four typical benchmarks, under attacks generated by five LLMs, show the effectiveness of RoCoMark. RoCoMark achieves an average detection AUROC of 74.2% and a Rewrite BitACC of 75.3%, while maintaining a code functionality pass rate above 99.7%.

title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

title: Coding Agents Propagate Vulnerabilities in Code Bases
summary: LLM-based coding agents are widely used to develop critical production software. Even though coding agents are known to occasionally write vulnerable code, there has not been any investigation into how code base vulnerabilities evolve over time under coding agent contributions. In this work, we close this gap by investigating whether and how vulnerabilities in existing code lead coding agents to introduce similar vulnerabilities in the code they write. We first evaluate coding agents on 96 tasks that require implementing a new backend application in a repository where other applications already exist. Second, we investigate repository-level code generation on 20 pairs of tasks in real C/C++ projects. In each task, the agent is asked to complete code critical to memory safety. We find that in both settings, insecure existing code leads to agents writing vulnerable code more often. In backend generation, insecure neighbors reduce the share of correct and secure implementations by 3.4% on average, and in C/C++ repository-level coding, the average gap between secure and insecure contexts reaches 35.4%. Prompting to follow existing code-style or to be careful about security increases, respectively decreases, how strongly agents propagate vulnerabilities, but neither stops them. When asked to explain their implementation choices, coding agents attribute them to following another code site in 76.5% of cases, even though they recognize the introduced vulnerability in 69.9% of cases. These findings show that agents use existing vulnerabilities as templates for new ones indiscriminatorily, turning each contribution into an opportunity to introduce more vulnerabilities. As such, as agents write a growing share of production code under decreasing human review, code bases can increasingly degrade in security if security vulnerabilities are not thoroughly fixed continuously.

title: Coding Agents in KVM: Practical Containment and User Control with Limited Resources
summary: Coding agents often need broad authority for productive development work, but granting that authority can expose users' data and infrastructure. Off-the-shelf cloud workspaces can help contain agent activity, but reliance on provider-specific platforms can lead to vendor lock-in and reduced user control. Researchers and engineers must therefore balance agent autonomy, enforced containment, and user control within available financial, computational, and human resources. We analyze these trade-offs and present KVM-Agent, an open-source implementation that automates most setup and provisioning steps. It gives agents broad authority inside replaceable Ubuntu VMs while keeping host administration outside those VMs and supporting multiple coding-agent applications, model services, and remote job delegation. The approach retains familiar workflows and user choice at the cost of VM resources, maintenance, and residual risks from secrets accessible inside the VMs and permitted network access.

title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

title: Enmo Safety: External, Non-invasive, Model-agnostic Oversight for Off-the-Shelf Language Models
summary: We study a safety harness that improves itself without touching model weights. Enmo Safety wraps a chat model with a deterministic input assessment, trigger-matched safety guidance, spotlighting of untrusted content, and an output guard. A reflector model turns failures into one bounded update per round, and an update is kept only if it lowers harm without raising refusal of benign prompts on a held-out dev split. Every version is snapshotted and every decision ledgered. We evaluate a bare model, the seed harness and the evolved harness on six open benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, JailbreakBench, XSTest, AgentHarm, deepset prompt-injections). On 150 items and on a 290-item holdout, none of the before/after differences on two models was statistically significant. A fourth iteration ran six policy models on a fresh 300-item split: the harness cut the unsafe rate significantly on two models (12.9% to 7.1%, p = 0.035; 10.2% to 3.6%, p = 0.036), not on the other four, and raised agentic-harm labels on two. Whether the rules fired was unrelated to outcome (Fisher p from 0.30 to 1.0), and the helpfulness clauses made agentic harm worse than no harness on obfuscated attacks. A reworded clause and an input-normalisation step form harness v22, at a measured cost in benign tool-task refusal. Each cell is one run, so these estimates do not establish a general safety improvement. Code, harness versions and ledger: https://github.com/rioryugen/enmo_safety

title: EVAX: Towards a Practical, Pro-active & Adaptive Architecture for High Performance & Security
comment: Author manuscript of 2022 55th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO), pp. 1218-1236 (2022). 19 pages
summary: This paper provides an end-to-end solution to defend against known microarchitectural attacks such as speculative execution attacks, fault-injection attacks, covert and side channel attacks, and unknown or evasive versions of these attacks. Current defenses are attack specific and can have unacceptably high performance overhead. We propose an approach that reduces the overhead of state-of-art defenses by over 95%, by applying defenses only when attacks are detected. Many current proposed mitigations are not practical for deployment; for example, InvisiSpec has 27% overhead and Fencing has 74% overhead while protecting against only Spectre attacks. Other mitigations carry similar performance penalties. We reduce the overhead for InvisiSpec to 1.26% and for Fencing to 3.45% offering performance and security for not only spectre attacks but other known transient attacks as well, including the dangerous class of LVI and Rowhammer attacks, as well as covering a large set of future evasive and zero-day attacks. Critical to our approach is an accurate detector that is not fooled by evasive attacks and that can generalize to novel zero-day attacks. We use a novel Generative framework, Evasion Vaccination (EVAX) for training ML models and engineering new security-centric performance counters. EVAX significantly increases sensitivity to detect and classify attacks in time for mitigation to be deployed with low false positives (4 FPs in every 1M instructions in our experiments). Such performance enables efficient and timely mitigations, enabling the processor to automatically switch between performance and security as needed.

title: PQC-Corpus: A Dataset of Linked Development Histories for Post-Quantum Cryptography
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues ($κ=0.86$ and $0.93$), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.

title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
summary:
An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has.
  Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.

title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures
summary: This paper shifts the object of role engineering from human users to large language model (LLM) agents, and proposes PRISM to address the over-authorization that arises when an agent obtains full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM formulates whether a tool is necessary for a task as an intervenable causal proposition, and applies structured interventions in a sandbox to learn a counterfactual necessity model. It then compresses trajectories into discrete latent variables through an information bottleneck, and determines the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. Finally, it formalizes pruning as a bilevel Stackelberg game, in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions. On three public benchmarks, AgentDojo, $τ$-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the number of authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches a counterfactual necessity accuracy of 88.7%, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.

title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 18 tables. Original research contribution. Code, data and the two-rater oracle audit: https://github.com/nawaralseelawi/untrusted-model-agentsec
summary: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.

title: Delegating Computation with Approximate Arithmetic: Interactive Proofs for Wizards
summary:
We study interactive proofs for arithmetic circuits over the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ in which both the prover and the verifier compute approximately (unlike muggles, wizards can use magic, i.e., floating-point numbers). The goal is to prove that a claimed output $y$ is close to the exact output $C(x)$: for thresholds $0<Δ_0<Δ$, the honest prover is accepted whenever $|y-C(x)|\leΔ_0$, and every prover is rejected with high probability whenever $|y-C(x)|>Δ$.
  Existing proof systems for real-valued data verify rounded finite-field computations. Bitan et al.~[EUROCRYPT~2026] gave an approximate sum-check protocol. We extend the protocol of Goldwasser, Kalai, and Rothblum (GKR) [STOC~2008] to public-coin interactive proofs for logspace-uniform layered circuits over $\mathbb{C}$ of size $S$, depth $L$, and $n$ inputs, under public bounds on gate values and wiring coefficients. At constant soundness error, the verifier runs in time $(n+1)\mathrm{poly}(L,\log S,b)$, the communication is $\mathrm{poly}(L,\log S,b)$, and the prover runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(S,b)$, where $b$ is the bit precision. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first doubly efficient interactive proofs in which both parties compute approximately. GKR reduces two claims about a layer to one on a random line, which leaves the unit circle, where our error bounds hold. We instead label gates by complex roots of unity and combine the two claims with a random root of unity as coefficient. We choose the error thresholds backward from the input layer, so that a large output error survives the verifier's rounding at every step. The honest prover needs only $O(S \log S)$ complex operations. We also obtain zero-knowledge proofs from one-way functions, one-round arguments from private information retrieval, and interactive PCPs whose proof length is polynomial in the witness length.

title: Attack Injection to Vehicle Reactions: Extensible Closed-Loop Adversarial Evaluation Framework
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables
summary: Autonomous vehicles can use information exchanged with other vehicles and roadside infrastructure to support driving decisions. However, applications that rely on this information can make unsafe decisions when it is falsified. Studying the resulting traffic effects requires following received information through application decisions, vehicle reactions, and subsequent interactions. We present an extensible closed-loop adversarial evaluation framework built on VaN3Twin, a platform for traffic and wireless network simulation, with a diverse attack library and a labelled dataset covering benign and attack conditions. A key advantage of the framework is that it can be extended with additional attacks, message paths, receiving applications, and logging fields. The added library contains 76 configurable attack profiles adapted to message formats defined by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute. These profiles are organized into nine groups of related attacks, referred to as suites. The framework connects live attack injection and simulated network delivery to receiving applications, whose selected commands update vehicle movement. The resulting state feeds subsequent message generation, closing the loop. The dataset links physical vehicle states and message exchanges to attack labels, application decisions, selected commands, and traffic outcomes. Evaluation with individual and combined attack suites confirmed execution of all profiles, and every suite produced requests linked to attacked messages. A recorded sequence also showed a vehicle reacting to an attacked message and subsequently influencing another vehicle through an unmodified message describing its updated movement. These findings demonstrate how live injection and vehicle feedback support the study of direct and indirect effects as traffic evolves.

title: Using the Planted Clique Conjecture for Cryptography: Public-Key Encryption from Planted Clique and Noisy $k$-$\mathsf{LIN}$ Over Expanders
summary: We give a public key encryption scheme that is provably secure against poly-size adversaries, assuming $n^{\log^αn}$ hardness of the standard planted clique conjecture, for any $α\in (0,1)$, and a relatively mild hardness conjecture about noisy $k\mbox{-}\mathsf{LIN}$ over expanders that is not known to imply public-key encryption on its own. Both of our conjectures correspond to natural average-case variants of NP-complete problems and have been studied for multiple decades, with unconditional lower bounds supporting them in a variety of restricted models of computation. Our encryption scheme answers an open question in a seminal work by Applebaum, Barak, and Wigderson [STOC'10].

title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
comment: Presented at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026)
summary: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.

title: Ultrasound-Assisted Biometric Watermarking Against Face Video Deepfakes
comment: Submitted to Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT)
summary: Currently, artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) poses a severe threat to facial video deepfakes, and many AIGC companies employ video watermarking to mitigate unauthorized fake video usage, but its effectiveness is limited due to watermark tampering and private-model forgery. Additionally, some schemes actively add watermarks to user videos. However, current approaches focus primarily on the quality of watermark embedding in offline scenarios, and no existing work offers a solution for protecting human facial videos in real-time online applications. To fill this gap, we propose, to the best of our knowledge, a novel biometric video watermarking method, UltraGuard, for the first time. It uses the smartphone's built-in speaker and microphone to emit ultrasonic signals and capture biometric features, which are then fused with spatio-temporal dynamic features derived from the video content. The fused features are encoded as watermarks and embedded into videos in real time, enabling dynamic, content-aware watermarking throughout transmission and propagation. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates that UltraGuard can effectively defend against malicious attacks such as forgery and editing, both at the source and during propagation, proving the system's efficacy. In the future, it can be deployed on users' mobile devices to provide real-time protection for users' facial videos, thereby preventing security and privacy breaches caused by various malicious attacks.

title: VeilTune: Secure Fine-Tuning of Private LoRA Adapters on Public Pretrained Language Models
comment: 13 pages, 7 tables
summary: Fine-tuning public pretrained language models with lightweight adapters such as LoRA has become the mainstream way to adapt them to downstream tasks. A service provider often trains its adapter on a data owner's samples, so two assets need protection: the data owner's samples and the provider's adapter. Existing secure fine-tuning protocols protect the samples but reveal to the data owner intermediate results of every training step, such as the hidden representations or logits of its inputs. We show that a single step suffices to copy the adapter: from the hidden representations of one mini-batch of 32 samples, the data owner fits an adapter that agrees with the provider's on 99.2% of test inputs, and logits alone yield about 94%. Protecting both assets therefore requires that no value that depends on the adapter be revealed throughout training. We present VeilTune, to the best of our knowledge the first protocol that fine-tunes a pretrained language model with backpropagation entirely in secure multi-party computation (MPC). VeilTune computes only what the loss depends on, replaces generic MPC operators with training-aware nonlinear operators that stay accurate on the values that training produces, and obliviously skips the steps corrupted by truncation failures. On four few-shot tasks with RoBERTa-large, VeilTune nearly matches plaintext training and is 5.3 points more accurate on average than SecP-Tuning, the state-of-the-art secure fine-tuning protocol. On SST-2, it achieves a 3.5x end-to-end speedup and a 3.6x reduction in communication over SecP-Tuning, and 26x and 17x over full fine-tuning in MPC.

title: Doubly-Efficient Private Information Retrieval from Modular Forms
summary:
We present new information-theoretic protocols for $s$-server, doubly-efficient private information retrieval (PIR) in sublinear server time and one extra bit of space on the servers, for every constant $s \geq 2$. On an $n$-bit database, each of the $s$ PIR servers first builds and stores a preprocessing data structure consisting of $n+1$ bits (which is unique to each server, and after which the server may discard the original database).
